## Reading Supply and Demand Shifts

For each situation below, determine which curve shifts and in which direction, then determine what happens to the equilibrium *price* and *quantity*. If one of price or quantity cannot be determined without more information, say so.

a. Demand increases (shifts right), supply is unchanged.
b. Supply increases (shifts right), demand is unchanged.
c. Demand decreases (shifts left), supply is unchanged.
d. Supply decreases (shifts left), demand is unchanged.
e. Both demand and supply increase (both shift right) at the same time.
f. Demand increases while supply decreases at the same time.
g. The price of a close substitute for this good falls. What happens to this good's market?
h. The price of a key input used to produce this good rises. What happens to this good's market?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GRAY = "#595959"

Q = [0, 20]

# Baseline: D0: P = 20 - Q, S0: P = Q -> equilibrium (10, 10)
d0 = [20 - q for q in Q]
s0 = [q for q in Q]

# a: demand right (+5) -> eq (12.5, 12.5): price up, quantity up
d1 = [25 - q for q in Q]
# b: supply right (+5, in Q) -> S1: P = Q - 5 -> eq with D0 (12.5, 7.5): price down, quantity up
s1_q = [5, 20]
s1 = [q - 5 for q in s1_q]
# c: demand left (-5) -> eq with S0 (7.5, 7.5): price down, quantity down
d2 = [15 - q for q in Q]
# d: supply left (+5, in Q) -> S2: P = Q + 5 -> eq with D0 (7.5, 12.5): price up, quantity down
s2 = [q + 5 for q in Q]

panels = [
    ("(a) Demand up", d0, s0, [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (12.5, 12.5, GRAY)], d1, None),
    ("(b) Supply up", d0, s0, [Q, s1_q], [(10, 10, "black"), (12.5, 7.5, GRAY)], None, s1),
    ("(c) Demand down", d0, s0, [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (7.5, 7.5, GRAY)], d2, None),
    ("(d) Supply down", d0, s0, [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (7.5, 12.5, GRAY)], None, s2),
]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, subplot_titles=[p[0] for p in panels])
positions = [(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)]

for (title, d0_, s0_, xr, eqs, d_shift, s_shift), (row, col) in zip(panels, positions):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d0_, mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash"),
                              showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s0_, mode="lines", line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash"),
                              showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    if d_shift is not None:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_shift, mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
                                  showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    if s_shift is not None:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xr[1], y=s_shift, mode="lines", line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3),
                                  showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    for (qx, px, color) in eqs:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[qx], y=[px], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=8, color=color),
                                  showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"), row=row, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[0, 20], showticklabels=False, row=row, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 25], showticklabels=False, row=row, col=col)

fig.update_layout(width=620, height=560, plot_bgcolor="white")
fig.show()
```

a. Demand shifts *right*. Both equilibrium price and quantity *increase* (dashed lines show the
   original curves, black dot the original equilibrium, gray dot the new one).
b. Supply shifts *right*. Equilibrium price *decreases* while quantity *increases*.
c. Demand shifts *left*. Both equilibrium price and quantity *decrease*.
d. Supply shifts *left*. Equilibrium price *increases* while quantity *decreases*.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

# e: both up (D +5, S +8 in Q) -> eq (16.5, 8.5)
d1e = [25 - q for q in Q]
s1e_q = [8, 20]
s1e = [q - 8 for q in s1e_q]
# f: demand up, supply down (D +5, S +3 in Q) -> eq (11, 14)
s2f = [q + 3 for q in Q]
# g: same pattern as (c), framed as a substitute good's price falling
# h: same pattern as (d), framed as an input cost rising

panels2 = [
    ("(e) Both increase", [Q, s1e_q], [(10, 10, "black"), (16.5, 8.5, GRAY)], d1e, s1e, None),
    ("(f) Demand up, supply down", [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (11, 14, GRAY)], d1e, s2f, None),
    ("(g) Substitute's price falls", [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (7.5, 7.5, GRAY)], d2, None, None),
    ("(h) Input cost rises", [Q, Q], [(10, 10, "black"), (7.5, 12.5, GRAY)], None, s2, None),
]

fig2 = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, subplot_titles=[p[0] for p in panels2])

for (title, xr, eqs, d_shift, s_shift, _), (row, col) in zip(panels2, positions):
    fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d0, mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash"),
                               showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s0, mode="lines", line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash"),
                               showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    if d_shift is not None:
        fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xr[0], y=d_shift, mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
                                   showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    if s_shift is not None:
        fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xr[1], y=s_shift, mode="lines", line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3),
                                   showlegend=False), row=row, col=col)
    for (qx, px, color) in eqs:
        fig2.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[qx], y=[px], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=8, color=color),
                                   showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"), row=row, col=col)
    fig2.update_xaxes(range=[0, 20], showticklabels=False, row=row, col=col)
    fig2.update_yaxes(range=[0, 25], showticklabels=False, row=row, col=col)

fig2.update_layout(width=620, height=560, plot_bgcolor="white")
fig2.show()
```

e. Both curves shift *right*. Equilibrium *quantity* unambiguously *increases* (both shifts push
   quantity up), but equilibrium *price* is *ambiguous*, it depends on which shift is larger. The
   panel above shows one example where the supply increase dominates and price falls; if the demand
   increase had been larger instead, price could have risen.
f. Demand shifts *right* while supply shifts *left*. Equilibrium *price* unambiguously *increases*
   (both shifts push price up), but equilibrium *quantity* is *ambiguous*, it depends on which shift
   is larger.
g. A falling price for a substitute makes that substitute more attractive, so buyers switch away
   from this good, this good's *demand shifts left*. That is the same pattern as (c): both
   equilibrium price and quantity *decrease*.
h. A higher input cost makes this good more expensive to produce at every quantity, so *supply
   shifts left*. That is the same pattern as (d): equilibrium price *increases* while quantity
   *decreases*.

</details>

## Problem 1: Equilibrium and Price Supports

The table below shows the demand and supply schedules for soybeans.

| Price | Quantity Demanded | Quantity Supplied |
|---|---|---|
| $7.20 | 10 | 40 |
| $7.00 | 15 | 35 |
| $6.80 | 20 | 30 |
| $6.60 | 25 | 25 |
| $6.40 | 30 | 20 |
| $6.20 | 35 | 15 |

*Quantities are in thousands of bushels.*

a. What is the equilibrium price of soybeans?
b. How many thousand bushels will be exchanged at that price?
c. If the federal government supports a price of $7.00 per bushel, is there a shortage or a
   surplus, and how many thousand bushels?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GRAY = "#595959"

price = [7.20, 7.00, 6.80, 6.60, 6.40, 6.20]
qd = [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35]
qs = [40, 35, 30, 25, 20, 15]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=qd, y=price, mode="lines", name="Demand",
    line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
    hovertemplate="Quantity: %{x}<br>Price: $%{y}<extra></extra>"
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=qs, y=price, mode="lines", name="Supply",
    line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3),
    hovertemplate="Quantity: %{x}<br>Price: $%{y}<extra></extra>"
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[25], y=[6.60], mode="markers+text", text=["Equilibrium"], textposition="bottom right",
    marker=dict(size=11, color="black"), showlegend=False,
    hovertemplate="Equilibrium<br>Quantity: 25<br>Price: $6.60<extra></extra>"
))
fig.add_hline(y=7.00, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY,
              annotation_text="Price support: $7.00", annotation_position="top left")

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Quantity (thousand bushels)", yaxis_title="Price",
    width=520, height=400, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.7, y=1.15, orientation="h")
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.show()
```

a. Equilibrium price is *$6.60*, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
b. *25* thousand bushels are exchanged at equilibrium.
c. At the $7.00 price support, quantity demanded is 15 and quantity supplied is 35. That is a
   *surplus* of *20* thousand bushels, the government's price floor sits above equilibrium, so
   sellers offer more than buyers want at that price.

</details>

## Problem 2: Equilibrium with a Price Ceiling

The table below summarizes the market for principles of economics textbooks.

| Price | Quantity Demanded | Quantity Supplied |
|---|---|---|
| $40 | 4,200 | 200 |
| $50 | 2,200 | 600 |
| $60 | 1,200 | 1,200 |
| $70 | 700 | 2,000 |
| $80 | 550 | 3,000 |

a. What is the market equilibrium price and quantity?
b. A college places a $50 price ceiling on textbooks to control costs for students. How many
   textbooks actually get sold at that price?
c. While the ceiling is in effect, a new printing technology lowers production costs, shifting
   supply to the right. What happens to the number of textbooks actually sold?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GREEN = "#548235"
GRAY = "#595959"

price = [40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
qd = [4200, 2200, 1200, 700, 550]
qs0 = [200, 600, 1200, 2000, 3000]

# Supply after the new printing technology lowers costs (shifted right)
qs1 = [500, 900, 1500, 2300, 3300]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=qd, y=price, mode="lines", name="Demand",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=qs0, y=price, mode="lines", name="Supply (original)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=qs1, y=price, mode="lines", name="Supply (after cost decrease)",
                          line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)))
fig.add_hline(y=50, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY,
              annotation_text="Price ceiling: $50", annotation_position="bottom right")
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1200], y=[60], mode="markers+text", text=["Original equilibrium"],
                          textposition="top left", marker=dict(size=10, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[600], y=[50], mode="markers+text", text=["Qs (original)"],
                          textposition="bottom right", marker=dict(size=9, color=ORANGE),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[900], y=[50], mode="markers+text", text=["Qs (after)"],
                          textposition="top right", marker=dict(size=9, color=GREEN),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2200], y=[50], mode="markers+text", text=["Qd at ceiling"],
                          textposition="top left", marker=dict(size=9, color=BLUE),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Quantity (textbooks)", yaxis_title="Price",
    width=600, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.35, y=1.18, orientation="h", font=dict(size=10))
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[35, 85])
fig.show()
```

a. Equilibrium is *$60*, where quantity demanded and quantity supplied both equal *1,200*.
b. At the $50 ceiling, quantity demanded is 2,200 but quantity supplied is only 600. The number of
   textbooks actually sold is capped by the *shorter* side of the market, so only *600* get sold,
   even though far more students want one at that price. This leaves a shortage of 1,600 books.
c. A rightward shift in supply means more textbooks are supplied at every price, including $50. As
   long as the ceiling is still below the new equilibrium price, more textbooks get sold than
   before (still capped by supply, but a higher supply quantity), narrowing the shortage. In the
   graph above, quantity supplied at the $50 ceiling rises from *600* to *900*, so the shortage
   shrinks from 1,600 to *1,300* books.

</details>

## Problem 3: Concert Tickets and StubHub

A popular artist announces a stadium tour. Tickets go on sale through the venue at a fixed face
price of $150, but the stadium only has 50,000 seats.

a. Draw or describe what happens to the demand curve for this concert compared to a typical touring
   act, and explain why.
b. At the $150 face price, is the quantity of tickets demanded larger or smaller than the quantity
   supplied (50,000 seats)? What does that imply happens in a resale market like StubHub?
c. Suppose resale tickets end up selling for $600. Using the supply and demand model, explain why
   the resale price is so much higher than the face price, even though it is the same seats being
   sold.
d. *Discussion:* A small number of platforms (like Live Nation-Ticketmaster) control both primary
   ticket sales and much of the resale market for major tours, and have faced antitrust scrutiny
   over this. Does having one dominant platform change how well the basic supply-and-demand model
   predicts ticket prices? Why or why not?
e. Airline seats on a specific flight are also fixed in number once the plane is scheduled. Is the
   short-run supply curve for seats on a given flight similarly vertical? Given that, why do
   airline tickets not typically show up on a resale market the way concert tickets do?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GRAY = "#595959"

Q = [0, 90]

# Vertical supply: fixed 50,000 seats
supply_q = [50, 50]
supply_p = [0, 700]

# Typical touring act demand: P = 300 - 3Q
d_typical_p = [300 - 3*q for q in Q]
# This artist's demand (shifted right): P = 750 - 3Q
d_star_p = [750 - 3*q for q in Q]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=supply_q, y=supply_p, mode="lines", name="Supply (fixed seats)",
                          line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_typical_p, mode="lines", name="Demand: typical act",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_star_p, mode="lines", name="Demand: this artist",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[50], y=[150], mode="markers+text", text=["Face price"],
                          textposition="bottom left", marker=dict(size=11, color=BLUE),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[50], y=[600], mode="markers+text", text=["Resale price"],
                          textposition="top left", marker=dict(size=11, color=ORANGE),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Seats (thousands)", yaxis_title="Price",
    width=560, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.02, y=1.2, orientation="h", font=dict(size=10))
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 90])
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 700])
fig.show()
```

a. Demand for this concert shifts *far to the right* relative to a typical touring act; at every
   price, many more people want a ticket, because the artist's popularity increases how much value
   fans place on attending.
b. Supply is fixed at 50,000 seats no matter the price (a vertical supply curve, at least in the
   short run for a specific show date). If quantity demanded at $150 is far above 50,000, there is
   an *excess quantity demanded* at the face price, some people who want a ticket at $150 will not
   get one, which creates the incentive for a resale market to exist.
c. Because supply is fixed, the face price of $150 does not do the job of *rationing* the limited
   seats to only the people willing to pay the most. The resale price is close to the price at
   which quantity demanded actually equals quantity supplied (50,000) once the artificially low
   face price is removed, that market-clearing price reflects how much buyers are truly willing to
   pay for a scarce good.
d. *Open discussion.* The basic model still explains the *direction* of the price (fixed supply and
   high demand push price up), but a dominant platform may be able to set or influence prices and
   fees beyond what a fully competitive resale market would produce, which is a market power
   question the simple supply-and-demand model does not fully capture. This is a preview of ideas
   covered when we study market structure later in the course.
e. Yes, the number of seats on a specific flight is also fixed once the plane is set, so short-run
   supply for that one flight is *vertical* too, just like a single concert. The key difference is
   on the pricing and transfer side, airlines themselves practice extensive *dynamic pricing*,
   raising the fare many times as a flight fills up, so the airline (not a third party) captures
   most of the value that would otherwise go to scalpers. Airline tickets are also typically
   *non-transferable* (tied to a passenger's name and ID), which blocks a resale market from
   forming the way concert tickets can be resold. One more difference worth noting: a concert is
   *one* venue with a fixed number of seats, but "airline seats" as a market means many airlines
   choosing flight frequency, routes, and plane size. Looking across a whole market like that, and
   over a longer time frame, supply *does* start to look like a normal upward-sloping curve rather
   than a single vertical line, airlines can and do add more seats when prices (and profits) are
   high. The vertical-supply story applies best to one specific, already-scheduled flight in the
   very short run.

</details>

## Problem 4: The Used Car Market During a Computer Chip Shortage

In 2021, a global shortage of semiconductor chips forced automakers to slow down new car
production, since modern cars need chips to run everything from engines to infotainment systems.

a. What happens to the *supply* of new cars during the chip shortage? Which direction does the new
   car supply curve shift?
b. As new cars become harder to find, many buyers turn to the used car market instead. What happens
   to the *demand* curve for used cars, and why?
c. At the same time, some used car owners decide to hold onto their vehicles longer rather than
   sell, since replacing the car would be difficult and expensive. What happens to the *supply*
   curve for used cars?
d. Using your answers to (b) and (c), explain what happens to the equilibrium *price* of used cars.
   Can you say for certain what happens to the equilibrium *quantity* of used cars sold? Why or why
   not?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GRAY = "#595959"

Q = list(range(0, 61))

# New car market: supply shifts left (chip shortage), demand roughly unchanged
d_new_p = [30 - 0.5*q for q in Q]
s_new0_p = [0.5*q for q in Q]
s_new1_p = [0.5*q + 10 for q in Q]

# Used car market: demand shifts right (substitute), supply shifts left (owners hold on)
d_used0_p = [30 - 0.5*q for q in Q]
d_used1_p = [35 - 0.5*q for q in Q]
s_used0_p = [0.5*q for q in Q]
s_used1_p = [0.5*q + 10 for q in Q]

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("New Car Market", "Used Car Market"))

# Panel 1: new cars, supply shift left only
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_new_p, mode="lines", name="Demand",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), legendgroup="d"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s_new0_p, mode="lines", name="Supply (original)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash"), legendgroup="s0"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s_new1_p, mode="lines", name="Supply (shifted left)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3), legendgroup="s1"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[30], y=[15], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[20], y=[20], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color=GRAY),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"), row=1, col=1)

# Panel 2: used cars, both curves shift
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_used0_p, mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d_used1_p, mode="lines", name="Demand (shifted right)",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s_used0_p, mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=s_used1_p, mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3)), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[30], y=[15], mode="markers+text", text=["Original"],
                          textposition="bottom right", marker=dict(size=10, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[25], y=[22.5], mode="markers+text", text=["New"],
                          textposition="top left", marker=dict(size=10, color=GRAY),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"), row=1, col=2)

fig.update_layout(
    width=780, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.0, y=1.25, orientation="h", font=dict(size=10))
)
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="New cars (thousands)", showgrid=True, gridwidth=1,
                  gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 60], row=1, col=1)
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Used cars (thousands)", showgrid=True, gridwidth=1,
                  gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 60], row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Price ($ thousands)", showgrid=True, gridwidth=1,
                  gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 35], row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 35], row=1, col=2)
fig.show()
```

a. The chip shortage raises production costs and limits how many new cars manufacturers can
   actually build, so the new car *supply curve shifts left*.
b. With new cars scarce and often more expensive, used cars become a more attractive substitute, so
   the *demand curve for used cars shifts right*, more buyers want used cars at every price.
c. Owners who would normally sell (perhaps to buy a newer car) hold on instead, so fewer used cars
   are offered for sale at every price, the *supply curve for used cars shifts left*.
d. Both shifts, demand right and supply left, push the equilibrium *price* of used cars up
   unambiguously (which is exactly what happened in 2021 and 2022). Equilibrium *quantity* is
   ambiguous, the rightward demand shift pushes quantity up while the leftward supply shift pushes
   quantity down, so without knowing the relative size of each shift, we cannot say from the model
   alone whether more or fewer used cars actually changed hands. In practice, used car sales volume
   fell even as prices spiked, telling us the supply shift was the dominant force.

</details>

## Problem 5: The Ozempic Effect

A new class of prescription drugs (GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy) is approved for
weight loss, in addition to its original use for diabetes. Demand for these drugs surges rapidly,
driven by both word of mouth and social media, while manufacturers struggle to build enough
production capacity to keep up.

a. What happens to the demand curve for these drugs, and why?
b. In the short run, manufacturing capacity for a complex injectable drug cannot expand quickly.
   What does that imply about the shape of the short-run supply curve, and what happens to price and
   quantity as a result?
c. Patients who need the drug for diabetes (its original approved use) report trouble finding it in
   stock, even though production levels have not fallen. Using the model, explain how a demand shift
   alone can create a *shortage* for existing users, without any change in supply.
d. Over the following two years, manufacturers invest heavily in new factories and production lines,
   and competing drug makers enter the market with similar products. What happens to the supply
   curve over this longer time horizon, and what would you expect to happen to price?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GREEN = "#548235"
GRAY = "#595959"

Q = list(range(0, 66))

# Original: D0 through (30,100) slope -2
d0_p = [160 - 2*q for q in Q]

# S_short is steep (near-vertical): slope 50, through (30,100).
# Restricted to where 0 <= P <= 250 so the line doesn't dominate the chart.
s_short_q = [q for q in Q if 0 <= 50*q - 1400 <= 250]
s_short_p = [50*q - 1400 for q in s_short_q]

# After demand shock: D1 through (31,150) slope -2, same S_short
d1_p = [212 - 2*q for q in Q]

# Long run: S_long is much flatter (slope 5) and shifted well to the right, so it never crosses
# S_short within the plotted range, representing new capacity available at every price level
s_long_q = [q for q in Q if 5*q - 160 >= 0]
s_long_p = [5*q - 160 for q in s_long_q]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d0_p, mode="lines", name="Demand (before)",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Q, y=d1_p, mode="lines", name="Demand (after shock)",
                          line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=s_short_q, y=s_short_p, mode="lines", name="Supply (short run)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=s_long_q, y=s_long_p, mode="lines", name="Supply (long run)",
                          line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[30], y=[100], mode="markers+text", text=["Before"],
                          textposition="bottom left", marker=dict(size=10, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[31], y=[150], mode="markers+text", text=["Short-run spike"],
                          textposition="top right", marker=dict(size=10, color=GRAY),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[53], y=[106], mode="markers+text", text=["Long-run"],
                          textposition="bottom right", marker=dict(size=10, color=GREEN),
                          showlegend=False, hoverinfo="text"))

# Shortage: hold price at the original $100 level (insurance-negotiated price is sticky).
# Quantity supplied barely moves (near-vertical short-run supply), quantity demanded jumps to 56.
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[30, 56], y=[100, 100], mode="lines+markers",
                          line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dot"),
                          marker=dict(size=8, color=GRAY), showlegend=False,
                          hoverinfo="skip"))
fig.add_annotation(x=43, y=100, yshift=14, text="Shortage at old price", showarrow=False,
                    font=dict(size=11, color=GRAY))
fig.add_annotation(x=30, y=100, yshift=-16, text="Qs", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=10))
fig.add_annotation(x=56, y=100, yshift=-16, text="Qd", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=10))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Quantity", yaxis_title="Price",
    width=560, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.0, y=1.25, orientation="h", font=dict(size=10))
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 65])
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 250])
fig.show()
```

a. Demand shifts *right*, a new, large group of potential buyers (people seeking weight loss, not
   just diabetes management) enters the market, increasing quantity demanded at every price.
b. In the short run, supply is close to *fixed* (nearly vertical), since building new manufacturing
   capacity takes years. With demand shifting right against a nearly fixed short-run supply, the
   *price* rises sharply while *quantity* increases only modestly.
c. Even though the amount supplied has not decreased, the large rightward shift in demand means
   quantity demanded now exceeds quantity supplied at the old price. Because there is effectively a
   price ceiling in practice (insurance-negotiated prices, or simply a price that does not adjust
   instantly), this excess demand shows up as a *shortage*, existing patients cannot get the drug
   even though nothing about supply changed for them specifically. On the graph, holding the price
   at its original $100 level after demand shifts to D1 shows quantity supplied stuck near *30*
   (short-run supply barely moves) while quantity demanded jumps to *56*, a shortage of *26* units
   at that price.
d. As new factories come online and competitors enter, the *supply curve shifts right* over time.
   With demand still elevated but supply now catching up, we would expect the equilibrium *price to
   fall* from its earlier peak (and *quantity* to keep rising), which is the standard pattern for
   markets adjusting to a large demand shock over the longer run.

</details>
